From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: Weight-of-Thought Reasoning: Exploring Neural Network Weights for Enhanced LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can neural network weights be examined before inference to identify and enhance reasoning pathways in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Weight-of-Thought reasoning, a novel approach that analyzes neural network weights prior to inference to identify and structure latent reasoning pathways, leading to improved performance and interpretability on complex reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Weight-of-Thought reasoning represents a significant step toward more structured, efficient, and interpretable reasoning in neural networks by leveraging the weight space, offering a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
WoT reasoning outperforms traditional methods like Chain-of-Thought on diverse reasoning tasks, especially complex multi-step problems.
The WoT model achieves superior performance with only ~2M parameters, demonstrating high parameter efficiency compared to large LLM baselines (~175B parameters).
Ablation studies show that weight-directed guidance, graph-based message passing, node specialization, and iterative refinement are all critical components contributing to WoT's performance.
Internal analysis reveals node specialization and dynamic, task-adaptive information flow within the reasoning graph.
WoT's graph structure enables parallel processing and adaptive information routing, moving beyond sequential reasoning chains.
papers.limitation:
Generalization capability across all types of reasoning problems requires further investigation.
The all-to-all message passing mechanism scales quadratically with the number of reasoning nodes, posing potential scaling challenges.
Performance is contingent on the quality and diversity of the training data.
Integrating WoT principles directly within the architecture of extremely large, pre-existing language models presents non-trivial technical hurdles.
Evaluation primarily relies on accuracy and MSE metrics, which may not fully encompass all facets of reasoning quality.
future_direction: Investigating generalization across broader reasoning problem types.
Addressing the quadratic scaling challenge of the message passing mechanism.
Developing integration techniques for large pre-existing language models and broader evaluation metrics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities when prompted with strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT).However, these approaches focus on token-level output without considering internal weight dynamics.We introduce Weight-of-Thought (WoT) reasoning, a novel approach that examines neural network weights before inference to identify reasoning pathways.Unlike existing methods, WoT explores the weight space through graph-based message passing, multi-step reasoning processes, and attention mechanisms.Our implementation creates an interconnected graph of reasoning nodes.Experiments on diverse reasoning tasks (syllogistic, mathematical, algebraic, combinatorial, and geometric) demonstrate that WoT achieves superior performance compared to traditional methods, particularly for complex problems.This approach leads to both improved performance and greater interpretability of the reasoning process, offering a promising direction for enhancing LLM reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Mitigating Cognitive Inertia in Large Reasoning Models via Latent Spike Steering
papers.research_question: How can cognitive inertia (overthinking and reasoning rigidity) in Large Reasoning Models be mitigated by monitoring and steering latent dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes STARS, a training-free framework that detects Cognitive Pivots via L2 distance spikes in hidden states and uses geometric trajectory analysis to diagnose and steer reasoning in real-time, mitigating cognitive inertia.
papers.conclusion: STARS effectively mitigates cognitive inertia in LRMs by detecting latent spikes and steering reasoning trajectories, offering a robust, unsupervised mechanism to optimize the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
STARS improves accuracy while reducing unnecessary token usage across diverse reasoning benchmarks.
STARS mitigates both overthinking (inertia of motion) and reasoning rigidity (inertia of direction).
STARS generalizes to non-mathematical domains such as logical puzzles and scientific reasoning.
STARS achieves lower tail latency and higher decoding throughput compared to token-level baselines like DEER and ConCISE.
The framework is training-free and does not require fine-tuning, operating solely at inference time.
papers.limitation:
When the model terminates reasoning before any salient latent spike occurs, no intervention can be triggered.
A detected spike may occasionally redirect the model toward an incorrect alternative trajectory, reinforcing rather than rectifying the error.
Spike-based signals may be less pronounced or harder to exploit in models with compressed representations, limited capacity, or training objectives that encourage smoother internal dynamics.
papers.abstract: While Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable performance by scaling test-time compute, they frequently suffer from Cognitive Inertia, a failure pattern manifesting as either overthinking (inertia of motion) or reasoning rigidity (inertia of direction). Existing detection methods, typically relying on superficial textual heuristics like self-correction tokens, often fail to capture the model's unvoiced internal conflicts. To address this, we propose STARS (Spike-Triggered Adaptive Reasoning Steering), a training-free framework designed to rectify cognitive inertia by monitoring latent dynamics. STARS identifies Cognitive Pivots-critical moments of reasoning transition-by detecting distinct L2 distance spikes in the hidden states. Upon detection, the framework employs geometric trajectory analysis to diagnose the structural nature of the transition and injects state-aware language cues to steer the model in real-time. Our experiments across diverse benchmarks confirm that STARS efficiently curtails redundant loops while improving accuracy through the adaptive correction of erroneous trajectories. STARS offers a robust, unsupervised mechanism to optimize the reasoning process of LRMs without requiring additional fine-tuning.

papers.title: Fantastic Reasoning Behaviors and Where to Find Them: Unsupervised Discovery of the Reasoning Process
papers.research_question: How can we discover reasoning behaviors in large language models without human supervision, and can these discovered behaviors be used to controllably steer reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RISE, an unsupervised framework that uses sparse auto-encoders to discover reasoning vectors in LLM activations, enabling interpretation and control of reasoning behaviors without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The unsupervised framework RISE successfully discovers and enables control of reasoning behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable approach for interpretability and test-time adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
SAE decoder columns form clusters corresponding to human-interpretable reasoning behaviors such as reflection and backtracking.
Interventions on SAE-derived vectors can controllably amplify or suppress specific reasoning behaviors during inference without retraining.
SAEs capture structural properties of reasoning, such as response length, with clear separation in mid-to-late layers.
SAEs can discover novel behaviors not predefined by humans, such as confidence-related vectors that influence reasoning style.
The learned reasoning vectors generalize across different data domains (e.g., from math to commonsense reasoning).
future_direction: Scalable unsupervised discovery of reasoning behaviors.
Dynamic test-time adaptation using discovered vectors.
Alignment of structural and semantic features for reliable reasoning.
papers.abstract: Despite the growing reasoning capabilities of recent large language models (LLMs), their internal mechanisms during the reasoning process remain underexplored. Prior approaches often rely on human-defined concepts (e.g., overthinking, reflection) at the word level to analyze reasoning in a supervised manner. However, such methods are limited, as it is infeasible to capture the full spectrum of potential reasoning behaviors, many of which are difficult to define in token space. In this work, we propose an unsupervised framework (namely, RISE: Reasoning behavior Interpretability via Sparse auto-Encoder) for discovering reasoning vectors, which we define as directions in the activation space that encode distinct reasoning behaviors. By segmenting chain-of-thought traces into sentence-level 'steps' and training sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) on step-level activations, we uncover disentangled features corresponding to interpretable behaviors such as reflection and backtracking. Visualization and clustering analyses show that these behaviors occupy separable regions in the decoder column space. Moreover, targeted interventions on SAE-derived vectors can controllably amplify or suppress specific reasoning behaviors, altering inference trajectories without retraining. Beyond behavior-specific disentanglement, SAEs capture structural properties such as response length, revealing clusters of long versus short reasoning traces. More interestingly, SAEs enable the discovery of novel behaviors beyond human supervision. We demonstrate the ability to control response confidence by identifying confidence-related vectors in the SAE decoder space. These findings underscore the potential of unsupervised latent discovery for both interpreting and controllably steering reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: When Thinking Backfires: Mechanistic Insights Into Reasoning-Induced Misalignment
papers.abstract: With the growing accessibility and wide adoption of large language models, concerns about their safety and alignment with human values have become paramount. In this paper, we identify a concerning phenomenon: Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), in which misalignment emerges when reasoning capabilities strengthened-particularly when specific types of reasoning patterns are introduced during inference or training. Beyond reporting this vulnerability, we provide the first mechanistic account of its origins. Through representation analysis, we discover that specific attention heads facilitate refusal by reducing their attention to CoT tokens, a mechanism that modulates the model's rationalization process during inference. During training, we find significantly higher activation entanglement between reasoning and safety in safety-critical neurons than in control neurons, particularly after fine-tuning with those identified reasoning patterns. This entanglement strongly correlates with catastrophic forgetting, providing a neuron-level explanation for RIM.

papers.title: A Statistical Physics of Language Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we model and understand the continuous-time reasoning dynamics of transformer language models using a statistical physics framework?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a statistical physics framework using stochastic differential equations and a Switching Linear Dynamical System to model and simulate reasoning dynamics in language models, enabling the prediction of misaligned states and failure modes.
papers.conclusion: The SLDS framework provides a tractable and interpretable model for reasoning dynamics, offering tools to study and predict critical transitions such as misaligned states in language models.
papers.key_findings:
A rank-40 projection captures 50% of the variance in sentence-level hidden state trajectories.
Four latent reasoning regimes are identified through Gaussian Mixture Model clustering of residuals.
The SLDS model accurately predicts reasoning dynamics and outperforms single-regime linear models in one-step-ahead prediction.
The framework shows transferability across models and tasks, though performance degrades across different model architectures.
In a case study, the SLDS successfully models and predicts adversarially induced belief shifts, demonstrating its utility for failure mode analysis.
future_direction: Future work could explore learning more invariant reasoning representations for better generalization.
papers.abstract: Transformer LMs show emergent reasoning that resists mechanistic understanding. We offer a statistical physics framework for continuous-time chain-of-thought reasoning dynamics. We model sentence-level hidden state trajectories as a stochastic dynamical system on a lower-dimensional manifold. This drift-diffusion system uses latent regime switching to capture diverse reasoning phases, including misaligned states or failures. Empirical trajectories (8 models, 7 benchmarks) show a rank-40 projection (balancing variance capture and feasibility) explains ~50% variance. We find four latent reasoning regimes. An SLDS model is formulated and validated to capture these features. The framework enables low-cost reasoning simulation, offering tools to study and predict critical transitions like misaligned states or other LM failures.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: How Likely Do LLMs with CoT Mimic Human Reasoning?
papers.research_question: How do LLMs with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) compare to human reasoning in terms of causal structure between instruction, reasoning steps, and answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs with CoT often deviate from ideal causal chains, showing spurious correlations; in-context learning strengthens causal structure, while supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning weaken it.
papers.conclusion: LLMs with CoT do not always mimic human reasoning perfectly, indicating a need for new techniques to improve reasoning processes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit four types of Structural Causal Models (SCMs): causal chain, common cause, full connection, and isolation.
Spurious correlations between instruction and answer lead to consistency errors and unfaithful reasoning.
In-context learning (ICL) strengthens the causal structure, but supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) weaken it.
Larger model size does not necessarily lead to stronger causal structures or better reasoning.
The type of SCM predicts the likelihood of consistency errors and faithfulness in reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Focus on basic CoT, leaving analysis of advanced methods like tree-of-thought for future work.
Coarse-grained analysis with only three variables; fine-grained structures are not considered.
future_direction: Analysis of advanced CoT methods such as tree-of-thought and graph-of-thought.
More detailed analysis of fine-grained reasoning structures.
Enhancing causal structures in LLMs during training using counterfactual examples or causal regulation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought emerges as a promising technique for eliciting reasoning capabilities from Large Language Models (LLMs). However, it does not always improve task performance or accurately represent reasoning processes, leaving unresolved questions about its usage. In this paper, we diagnose the underlying mechanism by comparing the reasoning process of LLMs with humans, using causal analysis to understand the relationships between the problem instruction, reasoning, and the answer in LLMs. Our empirical study reveals that LLMs often deviate from the ideal causal chain, resulting in spurious correlations and potential consistency errors (inconsistent reasoning and answers). We also examine various factors influencing the causal structure, finding that in-context learning with examples strengthens it, while post-training techniques like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on human feedback weaken it. To our surprise, the causal structure cannot be strengthened by enlarging the model size only, urging research on new techniques. We hope that this preliminary study will shed light on understanding and improving the reasoning process in LLM.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: Feature Extraction and Steering for Enhanced Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs without external datasets by extracting features from vanilla Chain-of-Thought and steering internal states?
papers.core_contribution: A framework that extracts reasoning features from vanilla CoT via verbal/symbolic decomposition and steers LLM activations to enhance reasoning without external datasets or retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature extraction and steering methods enhance reasoning in LLMs, and the SAE-free approach extends the benefits to models without corresponding SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based steering improves accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
SAE-free steering works without pre-trained SAEs and achieves comparable or better performance.
Steering increases reasoning length and attention to mathematical tokens.
There is an optimal steering strength; too high strength degrades performance.
The method suppresses noisy features and amplifies task-relevant reasoning features.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to mathematical reasoning datasets.
Experiments are limited to three model families (LLaMA, DeepSeek, Gemma).
future_direction: Extend to more diverse reasoning domains such as logical reasoning, scientific problem-solving, or multi-step planning.
Apply the method to more diverse LLM architectures to verify generalizability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate the ability to solve reasoning and mathematical problems using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) technique. Expanding CoT length, as seen in models such as DeepSeek-R1, significantly enhances this reasoning for complex problems, but requires costly and high-quality long CoT data and fine-tuning. This work, inspired by the deep thinking paradigm of DeepSeek-R1, utilizes a steering technique to enhance the reasoning ability of an LLM without external datasets. Our method first employs Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features from vanilla CoT. These features are then used to steer the LLM's internal states during generation. Recognizing that many LLMs do not have corresponding pre-trained SAEs, we further introduce a novel SAE-free steering algorithm, which directly computes steering directions from the residual activations of an LLM, obviating the need for an explicit SAE. Experimental results demonstrate that both our SAE-based and subsequent SAE-free steering algorithms significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: MARCOS: Deep Thinking by Markov Chain of Continuous Thoughts
papers.research_question: How can we re-imagine reasoning in large language models to overcome the drawbacks of token-based chain-of-thought, such as slow inference, information bottleneck, and entangled thinking and speaking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MARCOS, a new paradigm that models reasoning as a Markov chain of continuous thoughts, decoupling thinking from speaking, which achieves performance comparable to or better than token-based chain-of-thought with significant inference speedup.
papers.conclusion: MARCOS presents a new paradigm for latent thinking in LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art reasoning performance and efficiency, while enabling step-level control over randomness and opening avenues for reinforcement learning and non-autoregressive decoding.
papers.key_findings:
MARCOS outperforms all continuous reasoning baselines and surpasses token-based CoT by 4.7% on GSM8K with up to 15.7x inference speedup.
The random variable R_k controls different aspects of reasoning, such as output length and format, without compromising accuracy.
MARCOS supports non-autoregressive decoding in the speaking stage, maintaining competitive accuracy.
Ablation studies show that deep thinking neurons, random variables, and sparsity loss are all critical components.
The model generalizes well to out-of-domain benchmarks like SVAMP and MultiArith.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily focus on mathematical reasoning tasks.
Evaluation is conducted on relatively basic mathematical problems rather than more challenging datasets like MATH or AIME.
The model is trained from scratch and lacks pretraining on massive corpora, limiting its broader capabilities.
future_direction: Develop a pretraining methodology for MARCOS on large, unstructured corpora.
Explore reinforcement learning algorithms that leverage step-level control over randomness for efficient exploration.
Integrate more advanced non-autoregressive decoding strategies to further accelerate inference.
papers.abstract: The current paradigm for reasoning in large language models (LLMs) involves models "thinking out loud" via a sequence of tokens, known as chain-of-thought (CoT). This approach, while effective, has several significant drawbacks. Firstly, inference requires autoregressive generation of often thousands of CoT tokens, which is slow and computationally expensive. Secondly, it constrains reasoning to the discrete space of tokens, creating an information bottleneck across reasoning steps. Thirdly, it fundamentally entangles reasoning with token generation, forcing LLMs to "think while speaking," which causes potentially short-sighted reasoning. In light of these limitations, we re-imagine reasoning in LLMs and present a new paradigm: MARCOS. In our approach, rather than autoregressively generating tokens, we model reasoning as a hidden Markov chain of continuous, high-dimensional "thoughts". Each reasoning step involves a transition of the internal thoughts, where explicit reasoning steps (which may consist of hundreds of tokens) serve as observable variables, which are windows to peek into the implicit thoughts. Since this latent process is incompatible with the standard supervised learning, we further propose a two-phase variational training scheme. Our experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MARCOS outperforms existing continuous reasoning methods and, for the first time, achieves performance comparable to token-based CoT, even surpassing it by 4.7% on GSM8K with up to 15.7x speedup in inference. Beyond this, MARCOS offers additional advantages, such as step-level instead of token-level control over randomness, opening significant opportunities for reinforcement learning and reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Understanding and Steering the Cognitive Behaviors of Reasoning Models at Test-Time
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks. While effective, these trajectories are frequently inefficient, leading to high latency from excessive token generation, or unstable reasoning that alternates between underthinking (shallow, inconsistent steps) and overthinking (repetitive, verbose reasoning). In this work, we study the structure of reasoning trajectories and uncover specialized attention heads that correlate with distinct cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. By lightly intervening on these heads at inference time, we can steer the model away from inefficient modes. Building on this insight, we propose CREST, a training-free method for Cognitive REasoning Steering at Test-time. CREST has two components: (1) an offline calibration step that identifies cognitive heads and derives head-specific steering vectors, and (2) an inference-time procedure that rotates hidden representations to suppress components along those vectors. CREST adaptively suppresses unproductive reasoning behaviors, yielding both higher accuracy and lower computational cost. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks and models, CREST improves accuracy by up to 17.5% while reducing token usage by 37.6%, offering a simple and effective pathway to faster, more reliable LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models
papers.research_question: Do reasoning traces exhibit consistent structure when abstracted into functional episodes? How do reasoning dynamics differ across models? How do episode patterns correlate with correctness and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThinkARM, a framework for abstracting reasoning traces into functional episodes, enabling systematic analysis of reasoning structure and dynamics in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.
papers.key_findings:
Episode-level analysis reveals a functional progression from abstract reasoning to concrete execution to evaluative control.
Reasoning models distribute effort across analysis, exploration, execution, and verification, while non-reasoning models are heavily execution-focused.
Exploration serves as a critical branching point: correct solutions route exploration into monitoring or re-analysis, while incorrect ones tend to continue execution or terminate.
Efficient reasoning methods selectively suppress evaluation-oriented episodes and feedback loops, diverging from base model patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly expose reasoning traces, yet their underlying cognitive structure and steps remain difficult to identify and analyze beyond surface-level statistics. We adopt Schoenfeld's Episode Theory as an inductive, intermediate-scale lens and introduce ThinkARM (Anatomy of Reasoning in Models), a scalable framework that explicitly abstracts reasoning traces into functional reasoning steps such as Analysis, Explore, Implement, Verify, etc. When applied to mathematical problem solving by diverse models, this abstraction reveals reproducible thinking dynamics and structural differences between reasoning and non-reasoning models, which are not apparent from token-level views. We further present two diagnostic case studies showing that exploration functions as a critical branching step associated with correctness, and that efficiency-oriented methods selectively suppress evaluative feedback steps rather than uniformly shortening responses. Together, our results demonstrate that episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.

papers.title: On the Representational Capacity of Neural Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the representational capacity of neural language models (LMs) when augmented with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning? Specifically, can CoT-augmented LMs represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in a probabilistic setting and shows that recurrent and transformer language models augmented with CoT reasoning can represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning increases the computational power of neural language models by allowing them to perform additional sequential computation and keep track of execution trajectories, effectively introducing non-determinism and enabling simulation of probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.key_findings:
CoT-augmented constant-precision RNN LMs are equivalent to probabilistic finite-state automata (PFSAs), whereas without CoT they are equivalent to deterministic PFSAs.
CoT-augmented RNN LMs with linearly bounded precision and transformer LMs with logarithmically bounded precision can simulate any probabilistic Turing machine.
CoT reasoning provides a principled way to overcome the limitation of deterministic computation in fixed-precision neural models, allowing them to simulate non-deterministic automata.

papers.title: How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concepts of validity and plausibility, and why do they conflate them, leading to content effects in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that validity and plausibility are linearly represented and aligned in LLMs, causing content effects, and that steering vectors can disentangle these concepts to reduce bias and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The representational entanglement of validity and plausibility in LLMs leads to content effects, and representational interventions offer a way to mitigate these biases for more logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit content effects where plausibility influences validity judgments, especially in zero-shot settings.
Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded as single directions in the model's activation space, and these vectors are highly similar.
The degree of alignment between validity and plausibility vectors predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models.
Plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgments, and vice versa, demonstrating cross-concept influence.
Debiasing steering vectors that disentangle validity from plausibility can reduce content effects and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.abstract: Both humans and large language models (LLMs) exhibit content effects: biases in which the plausibility of the semantic content of a reasoning problem influences judgments regarding its logical validity. While this phenomenon in humans is best explained by the dual-process theory of reasoning, the mechanisms behind content effects in LLMs remain unclear. In this work, we address this issue by investigating how LLMs encode the concepts of validity and plausibility within their internal representations. We show that both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry, leading models to conflate plausibility with validity. Using steering vectors, we demonstrate that plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgements, and vice versa, and that the degree of alignment between these two concepts predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models. Finally, we construct debiasing vectors that disentangle these concepts, reducing content effects and improving reasoning accuracy. Our findings advance understanding of how abstract logical concepts are represented in LLMs and highlight representational interventions as a path toward more logical systems.

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in LLMs through Information Theory
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the quality of each step in a model's Chain-of-Thought reasoning without requiring annotated step-by-step data, in order to identify failure modes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic framework to quantify the 'information-gain' at each step of a Chain-of-Thought reasoning process, enabling the identification of reasoning failures without the need for expensive annotated step-by-step data.
papers.conclusion: The information-theoretic framework provides a rigorous and practical method for evaluating Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, enabling granular failure detection without the need for costly annotated data.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Information-Gain method accurately identifies incorrect reasoning steps in Chain-of-Thought, outperforming baseline methods like Outcome Reward Modeling and Math-Shepherd.
The method is effective in detecting errors even when the correctness of a step depends on previous steps, a scenario where baselines fail.
It does not require annotated Chain-of-Thought data, making it more scalable than process-based supervision methods.
The framework is validated on synthetic data, GSM8K, and PRM800k datasets, showing consistent performance across different complexities.
The information-gain metric can be applied to both linear and exploratory (e.g., O1/R1-style) reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in complex reasoning tasks through the use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, allowing models to break down problems into manageable sub-tasks. However, existing CoT evaluation techniques either require annotated CoT data or fall short in accurately assessing intermediate reasoning steps, leading to high rates of false positives. In this paper, we formalize CoT reasoning in LLMs through an information-theoretic lens. Specifically, our framework quantifies the `information-gain' at each reasoning step, enabling the identification of failure modes in LLMs without the need for expensive annotated datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on toy arithmetic, GSM8K and PRM800k datasets, where it significantly outperforms existing outcome-based methods by providing more accurate insights into model performance on individual subtasks.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally perform a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements a backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree one level per layer, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a certain depth, using parallelized strategies and heuristics, which provides insights into the operating principles of transformers for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head concatenates edge tokens by copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers perform backward chaining, moving one step up the tree per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining from multiple subgoals and merges subpaths.
The model uses a one-step lookahead heuristic to identify child nodes and avoid leaf nodes when backward chaining is insufficient.
The model's reasoning is depth-bounded and resorts to heuristics beyond its depth limit.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a synthetic symbolic reasoning task and may not directly translate to natural language tasks.
The input format uses shuffled edge lists in backward order, and the mechanisms might vary for other arrangements.
papers.abstract: Transformers demonstrate impressive performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks. To evaluate the degree to which these abilities are a result of actual reasoning, existing work has focused on developing sophisticated benchmarks for behavioral studies. However, these studies do not provide insights into the internal mechanisms driving the observed capabilities. To improve our understanding of the internal mechanisms of transformers, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of a transformer trained on a synthetic reasoning task. We identify a set of interpretable mechanisms the model uses to solve the task, and validate our findings using correlational and causal evidence. Our results suggest that it implements a depth-bounded recurrent mechanisms that operates in parallel and stores intermediate results in selected token positions. We anticipate that the motifs we identified in our synthetic setting can provide valuable insights into the broader operating principles of transformers and thus provide a basis for understanding more complex models.

papers.title: Emergence of Superposition: Unveiling the Training Dynamics of Chain of Continuous Thought
papers.research_question: How does the superposition mechanism in chain of continuous thought emerge during gradient-based training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient-based training of continuous CoT leads to bounded attention logits (index-matching logit), which enables superposition and balances exploration and exploitation in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Gradient-based training naturally leads to superposition in continuous CoT, with bounded attention logits playing a key role in balancing exploration and exploitation during reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Under COCONUT training, the index-matching logit remains bounded, unlike in discrete settings where it diverges.
Bounded logits allow the model to maintain a superposition of multiple plausible reasoning traces.
The bounded logit balances exploration and exploitation: it exploits local graph structure while exploring multiple paths.
In the thought generation stage, the model performs one-step expansion, aggregating reachable nodes into the continuous thought.
In the prediction stage, the model learns to combine residual carryover and candidate lift signals to correctly predict the reachable node.
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis is limited to a simplified two-layer transformer with orthonormal embeddings.
future_direction: Extending the theoretical analysis to deeper transformers and more complex tasks.
Comprehensive study of hyperparameter interactions in training.
papers.abstract: Previous work shows that the chain of continuous thought (continuous CoT) improves the reasoning capability of large language models (LLMs) by enabling implicit parallel thinking, and a subsequent work provided theoretical insight by showing that a two-layer transformer equipped with continuous CoT can efficiently solve directed graph reachability by maintaining a superposition of multiple reasoning traces in the continuous thought. However, it remains unclear how the superposition mechanism is naturally learned from gradient-based training methods. To fill this gap, we theoretically analyze the training dynamics of a simplified two-layer transformer on the directed graph reachability problem to unveil how the superposition mechanism emerges during training in two training stages -- (i) a thought-generation stage that autoregressively expands the continuous thought, and (ii) a prediction stage that converts the thought into the final answer. Our analysis reveals that during training using continuous thought, the index-matching logit, an important quantity which reflects the strength of the model's local search ability, will first increase and then remain bounded under mild assumptions. The bounded index-matching logit effectively balances exploration and exploitation during the reasoning process: the model will exploit local problem structures to identify plausible search traces, and assign comparable weights to multiple such traces to explore when it is uncertain about which solution is correct, which results in superposition. Our experimental results tracking the growth of logits further validate our theory.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for State Dynamics in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the limits to using the residual stream to capture state-dynamics as the number of states and transition constraints scale? How can mechanistic interpretability provide causal explanations for why predicting state-dynamics fails at certain scales? What mechanisms or circuits in LLMs particularly model sequential state-dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematically studies how transformer-based LLMs represent and update internal state across three synthetic domains, using mechanistic interpretability to identify the components and mechanisms responsible for state-tracking behavior.
papers.conclusion: State-tracking in LLMs is a behavior resulting from different types of attention heads working together, involving an initial phase of Induction Head formation and a subsequent phase of Induction Head optimization, with larger models showing more effective formation of Name-Mover Heads.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models within a family generally exhibit better accuracy on state-tracking tasks, suggesting increased capacity aids in tracking and updating entity states.
Activation patching identifies specific attention heads in later layers that are crucial for state-tracking, such as those attending to tokens related to the queried object's final destination.
In the Abstract DFA task, state-tracking appears limited to pattern matching without robust attention across state-action history.
Critical heads for state-tracking include 'Induction Heads' that attend to previous state occurrences and 'Name-Mover Heads' that associate states with objects.
State-tracking is not led by an individual attention head but is the result of different types of attention heads (e.g., Induction Heads and Name-Mover Heads) working together.
future_direction: A deeper exploration of Name-Mover Heads, focusing on identifying the factors aiding in their emergence.
More thorough patching techniques, such as path patching, to reinforce the results.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in tasks requiring internal state tracking, yet their ability to model state transition dynamics remains poorly understood. We evaluate how well LLMs capture deterministic state dynamics across 3 domains: Box Tracking, Abstract DFA Sequences, and Complex Text Games, each formalizable as a finite-state system. Across tasks, we find that next-state prediction accuracy degrades with increasing state-space size and sparse transitions. GPT-2 XL reaches about 70% accuracy in low-complexity settings but drops below 30% when the number of boxes or states exceeds 5 or 10, respectively. In DFA tasks, Pythia-1B fails to exceed 50% accuracy when the number of states is > 10 and transitions are < 30. Through activation patching, we identify attention heads responsible for propagating state information: GPT-2 XL Layer 22 Head 20, and Pythia-1B Heads at Layers 10, 11, 12, and 14. While these heads successfully move relevant state features, action information is not reliably routed to the final token, indicating weak joint state-action reasoning. Our results suggest that state tracking in LLMs emerges from distributed interactions of next-token heads rather than explicit symbolic computation.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: From Chains to DAGs: Probing the Graph Structure of Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of LLMs encode graph-structured reasoning (as directed acyclic graphs) beyond linear chains, and where does this structure emerge across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework to test whether LLM hidden states linearly encode reasoning DAG structure, and finds that such structure is meaningfully encoded, peaking in intermediate layers, and varies with node depth, edge span, and model scale.
papers.conclusion: LLM reasoning is not purely sequential, but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.
papers.key_findings:
DAG structure is meaningfully encoded in LLM representations.
Recoverability of DAG structure peaks in intermediate layers.
Recovery varies systematically by node depth, edge span, and model scale.
The framework enables nontrivial recovery of dependency graphs.
Larger models achieve higher recoverability, and reasoning-oriented training recipes provide modest gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on frozen pretrained models; it remains open whether fine-tuning or reinforcement learning alters the internal geometry of reasoning.
The probing approach assumes that reasoning DAG structure is linearly accessible in hidden states; nonlinear or distributed encodings may require more expressive probes.
The DAG formalization for GSM8K relies on GPT-5 mini, which may introduce noise or bias.
future_direction: Extend the framework to dynamic or cyclic reasoning.
Incorporate more expressive probes.
Investigate how training interventions affect internal reasoning structure.
papers.abstract: Recent progress in large language models has renewed interest in mechanistically characterizing how multi-step reasoning is represented and computed. While much prior work treats reasoning as a linear chain of steps, many reasoning problems are more naturally structured as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where intermediate conclusions may depend on multiple premises, branch into parallel sub-derivations, and later merge or be reused. Understanding whether such graph-structured reasoning is reflected in model internals remains an open question. In this work, we introduce Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework that directly asks whether LLM hidden states encode the geometry of a reasoning DAG in a linearly accessible form, and where this structure emerges across layers. Within this framework, we associate each reasoning node with a textual realization and train lightweight probes to predict two graph-theoretic properties from hidden states: node depth and pairwise node distance. We use these probes to analyze the layerwise emergence of DAG structure and evaluate controls that disrupt reasoning-relevant structure while preserving superficial textual properties. Our results provide evidence that reasoning DAG geometry is meaningfully encoded in intermediate layers, with recoverability varying systematically by node depth and model scale, suggesting that LLM reasoning is not only sequential but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the behavior of large language models indicate belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring as defined by the HOT-3 indicator for consciousness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework and the Belief Dominance metric to test the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs, providing empirical evidence for belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the existence of agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs, contributing to the study of AI consciousness.
papers.key_findings:
External manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation.
Belief formation causally drives the model's action selection.
Models can monitor and report their own belief states, indicating meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic implementation of belief formation, action selection, and meta-cognition remains unclear.
The framework is restricted to capturing beliefs that can be expressed in words.
The framework currently only tests two competing beliefs.
future_direction: Studying the mechanistic implementation of belief formation and meta-cognitive monitoring.
Extending the framework to capture latent beliefs beyond existing vocabulary.
Testing additional consciousness criteria in more capable models.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.

papers.title: Mapping Faithful Reasoning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) traces promise transparency for reasoning language models, but prior work shows they are not always faithful reflections of internal computation. This raises challenges for oversight: practitioners may misinterpret decorative reasoning as genuine.
