Subsequently, we proposed a dynamic selection and optimization Chain-of-Thought framework, combining multi-candidate generation, a hybrid evaluation system (expert scoring and automated metrics) and a closed-loop iterative optimization mechanism, and fine-tuned the LLM for the second time based on the first finetuning. Experimental results show that the combination of Logical Fallacy Understanding and Diagnosis-Repaired (LFUD-R) and DSO-CoT frameworks produces significant synergistic effects on LogiQA, Reclor, and LogiQA2.0 datasets, further improving the model accuracy to 70.15%, 80.20%, and 71.93%. This study not only verifies the effectiveness of LFUD-R and DSO-CoT frameworks in improving the logical reasoning ability of LLM, but also reveals the important role of structured cognitive task design and reasoning framework optimization in enhancing the logical reasoning ability of models.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Augmentation with Logit Contrast for Enhanced Reasoning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Rapidly increasing model scales coupled with steering methods such as chain-of-thought prompting have led to drastic improvements in language model reasoning. At the same time, models struggle with compositional generalization and are far from human performance on many reasoning-based benchmarks. Leveraging the success of chain-of-thought prompting, and also taking inspiration from context-aware decoding (CAD), we explore input-based contrasting methods to further encourage the type of reasoning induced by chain-of-thought prompting. While work remains to stabilize these results across datasets and models, the improvements we find warrant further investigation into input-based steering methods for context-aware reasoning.

papers.title: Chain of Draft: Thinking Faster by Writing Less
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in solving complex reasoning tasks through mechanisms like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, which emphasizes verbose, step-by-step reasoning. However, humans typically employ a more efficient strategy: drafting concise intermediate thoughts that capture only essential information. In this work, we propose Chain of Draft (CoD), a novel paradigm inspired by human cognitive processes, where LLMs generate minimalistic yet informative intermediate reasoning outputs while solving tasks. By reducing verbosity and focusing on critical insights, CoD matches or surpasses CoT in accuracy while using as little as only 7.6% of the tokens, significantly reducing cost and latency across various reasoning tasks. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/sileix/chain-of-draft.

papers.title: Parallel Continuous Chain-of-Thought with Jacobi Iteration
papers.abstract: Continuous chain-of-thought has been shown to be effective in saving reasoning tokens for large language models. By reasoning with continuous latent thought tokens, continuous CoT is able to perform implicit reasoning in a compact manner. However, the sequential dependencies between latent thought tokens spoil parallel training, leading to long training time. In this paper, we propose Parallel Continuous Chain-of-Thought (PCCoT), which performs Jacobi iteration on the latent thought tokens, updating them iteratively in parallel instead of sequentially and thus improving both training and inference efficiency of continuous CoT. Experiments demonstrate that by choosing the proper number of iterations, we are able to achieve comparable or even better performance while saving nearly 50% of the training and inference time. Moreover, PCCoT shows better stability and robustness in the training process. Our code is available at https://github.com/whyNLP/PCCoT.

papers.title: Larger Language Models Don't Care How You Think: Why Chain-of-Thought Prompting Fails in Subjective Tasks
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) in Large Language Models (LLM) has emerged as the dominant technique for performing natural language tasks, as it does not require updating the model parameters with gradient-based methods. ICL promises to "adapt" the LLM to perform the present task at a competitive or state-of-the-art level at a fraction of the computational cost. ICL can be augmented by incorporating the reasoning process to arrive at the final label explicitly in the prompt, a technique called Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. However, recent work has found that ICL relies mostly on the retrieval of task priors and less so on "learning" to perform tasks, especially for complex subjective domains like emotion and morality, where priors ossify posterior predictions. In this work, we examine whether "enabling" reasoning also creates the same behavior in LLMs, wherein the format of CoT retrieves reasoning priors that remain relatively unchanged despite the evidence in the prompt. We find that, surprisingly, CoT indeed suffers from the same posterior collapse as ICL for larger language models. Code is avalaible at https://github.com/gchochla/cot-priors.

papers.title: Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification
papers.abstract: Recently, with the chain of thought (CoT) prompting, large language models (LLMs), e.g., GPT-3, have shown strong reasoning ability in several natural language processing tasks such as arithmetic, commonsense, and logical reasoning. However, LLMs with CoT require multi-step prompting and multi-token prediction, which is highly sensitive to individual mistakes and vulnerable to error accumulation. The above issues make the LLMs need the ability to verify the answers. In fact, after inferring conclusions in some thinking decision tasks, people often check them by re-verifying steps to avoid some mistakes. In this paper, we propose and prove that LLMs also have similar self-verification abilities. We take the conclusion obtained by CoT as one of the conditions for solving the original problem. By performing a backward verification of the answers that LLM deduced for itself, we can obtain interpretable answer validation scores to select the candidate answer with the highest score. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can improve the reasoning performance on various arithmetic, commonsense, and logical reasoning datasets. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/WENGSYX/Self-Verification.

papers.title: Expediting and Elevating Large Language Model Reasoning via Hidden Chain-of-Thought Decoding
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tasks requiring reasoning and multi-step problem-solving through the use of chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. However, generating the full CoT process results in significantly longer output sequences, leading to increased computational costs and latency during inference. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach to compress the CoT process through semantic alignment, enabling more efficient decoding while preserving the benefits of CoT reasoning. Our method introduces an auxiliary CoT model that learns to generate and compress the full thought process into a compact special token representation semantically aligned with the original CoT output. This compressed representation is then integrated into the input of the Hidden Chain-of-Thought (HCoT) model. The training process follows a two-stage procedure: First, the CoT model is optimized to generate the compressed token representations aligned with the ground-truth CoT outputs using a contrastive loss. Subsequently, with the CoT model parameters frozen, the HCoT model is fine-tuned to generate accurate subsequent predictions conditioned on the prefix instruction and the compressed CoT representations from the CoT model. Extensive experiments across three challenging domains - mathematical reasoning, agent invocation, and question answering - demonstrate that our semantic compression approach achieves competitive or improved performance compared to the full CoT baseline, while providing significant speedups of at least 1.5x in decoding time. Moreover, incorporating contrastive learning objectives further enhances the quality of the compressed representations, leading to better CoT prompting and improved task accuracy. Our work paves the way for more efficient exploitation of multi-step reasoning capabilities in LLMs across a wide range of applications.

papers.title: Self-Reflection on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: A strong capability of large language models is Chain-of-Thought reasoning. Prompting a model to ‘think step-by-step’ has led to great performance improvements in solving problems such as planning and question answering, and with the extended output it provides some evidence about the rationale behind an answer or decision. In search of better, more robust, and interpretable language model behavior, this work investigates self-reflection in large language models. Here, self-reflection consists of feedback from large language models to medical question-answering and whether the feedback can be used to accurately distinguish between correct and incorrect answers. GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 provide zero-shot feedback scores to Chain-of-Thought reasoning on the MedQA (medical questionanswering) dataset. The question-answering is evaluated on traits such as being structured, relevant and consistent. We test whether the feedback scores are different for questions that were either correctly or incorrectly answered by Chain-of-Thought reasoning. The potential differences in feedback scores are statistically tested with the Mann-Whitney U test. Graphical visualization and logistic regressions are performed to preliminarily determine whether the feedback scores are indicative to whether the Chain-of-Thought reasoning leads to the right answer. The results indicate that among the reasoning objectives, the feedback models assign higher feedback scores to questions that were answered correctly than those that were answered incorrectly. Graphical visualization shows potential for reviewing questions with low feedback scores, although logistic regressions that aimed to predict whether or not questions were answered correctly mostly defaulted to the majority class. Nonetheless, there seems to be a possibility for more robust output from self-reflecting language systems.

papers.title: Exchange-of-Thought: Enhancing Large Language Model Capabilities through Cross-Model Communication
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently made significant strides in complex reasoning tasks through the Chain-of-Thought technique. Despite this progress, their reasoning is often constrained by their intrinsic understanding, lacking external insights. To address this, we propose Exchange-of-Thought (EoT), a novel framework that enables cross-model communication during problem-solving. Drawing inspiration from network topology, EoT integrates four unique communication paradigms: Memory, Report, Relay, and Debate. This paper delves into the communication dynamics and volume associated with each paradigm. To counterbalance the risks of incorrect reasoning chains, we implement a robust confidence evaluation mechanism within these communications. Our experiments across diverse complex reasoning tasks demonstrate that EoT significantly surpasses established baselines, underscoring the value of external insights in enhancing LLM performance. Furthermore, we show that EoT achieves these superior results in a cost-effective manner, marking a promising advancement for efficient and collaborative AI problem-solving.

papers.title: Reassessing the Role of Chain-of-Thought in Sentiment Analysis: Insights and Limitations
papers.abstract: The relationship between language and thought remains an unresolved philosophical issue. Existing viewpoints can be broadly categorized into two schools: one asserting their independence, and another arguing that language constrains thought. In the context of large language models, this debate raises a crucial question: Does a language model's grasp of semantic meaning depend on thought processes? To explore this issue, we investigate whether reasoning techniques can facilitate semantic understanding. Specifically, we conceptualize thought as reasoning, employ chain-of-thought prompting as a reasoning technique, and examine its impact on sentiment analysis tasks. The experiments show that chain-of-thought has a minimal impact on sentiment analysis tasks. Both the standard and chain-of-thought prompts focus on aspect terms rather than sentiment in the generated content. Furthermore, counterfactual experiments reveal that the model's handling of sentiment tasks primarily depends on information from demonstrations. The experimental results support the first viewpoint.

papers.title: Focus on Your Question! Interpreting and Mitigating Toxic CoT Problems in Commonsense Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit high-level commonsense reasoning abilities, especially with enhancement methods like Chain-of-Thought (CoT). However, we find these CoT-like methods lead to a considerable number of originally correct answers turning wrong, which we define as the Toxic CoT problem. To interpret and mitigate this problem, we first utilize attribution tracing and causal tracing methods to probe the internal working mechanism of the LLM during CoT reasoning. Through comparisons, we prove that the model exhibits information loss from the question over the shallow attention layers when generating rationales or answers. Based on the probing findings, we design a novel method called RIDERS (Residual decodIng and sERial-position Swap), which compensates for the information deficit in the model from both decoding and serial-position perspectives. Through extensive experiments on multiple commonsense reasoning benchmarks, we validate that this method not only significantly eliminates Toxic CoT problems (decreased by 23.6%), but also effectively improves the model's overall commonsense reasoning performance (increased by 5.5%).

papers.title: Investigating Mysteries of CoT-Augmented Distillation
papers.abstract: Eliciting "chain of thought" (CoT) rationales -- sequences of token that convey a "reasoning" process -- has been shown to consistently improve LLM performance on tasks like question answering. More recent efforts have shown that such rationales can also be used for model distillation: Including CoT sequences (elicited from a large "teacher" model) in addition to target labels when fine-tuning a small student model yields (often substantial) improvements. In this work we ask: Why and how does this additional training signal help in model distillation? We perform ablations to interrogate this, and report some potentially surprising results. Specifically: (1) Placing CoT sequences after labels (rather than before) realizes consistently better downstream performance -- this means that no student "reasoning" is necessary at test time to realize gains. (2) When rationales are appended in this way, they need not be coherent reasoning sequences to yield improvements; performance increases are robust to permutations of CoT tokens, for example. In fact, (3) a small number of key tokens are sufficient to achieve improvements equivalent to those observed when full rationales are used in model distillation.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: Explainable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: An Empirical Analysis on State-Aware Reasoning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we abstract and model the latent structure of chain-of-thought reasoning to provide a global, explainable view of reasoning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a state-aware transition framework that abstracts chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories into structured latent dynamics via spectral analysis and Markov chains, enabling a global, explainable view of reasoning steps and transitions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a global perspective on multi-step reasoning in LLMs, uncovering consistent latent structures across models and tasks, and enables explainability applications for CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully abstracts CoT reasoning steps into semantically coherent latent states via spectral embeddings and clustering.
Learned transition patterns are consistent across models and tasks, indicating structured reasoning dynamics beyond surface token sequences.
The latent states correspond to meaningful functional roles (e.g., scenario description, problem framing, answer synthesis).
The Markov chain model captures coherent temporal reasoning flows, validated by Monte Carlo simulations.
The approach enables explainability applications such as semantic role identification and temporal pattern visualization.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes access to internal representations of open-source language models.
It focuses primarily on intrinsic structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting have enabled large language models (LLMs) to perform multi-step reasoning. However, the explainability of such reasoning remains limited, with prior work primarily focusing on local token-level attribution, such that the high-level semantic roles of reasoning steps and their transitions remain underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a state-aware transition framework that abstracts CoT trajectories into structured latent dynamics. Specifically, to capture the evolving semantics of CoT reasoning, each reasoning step is represented via spectral analysis of token-level embeddings and clustered into semantically coherent latent states. To characterize the global structure of reasoning, we model their progression as a Markov chain, yielding a structured and interpretable view of the reasoning process. This abstraction supports a range of analyses, including semantic role identification, temporal pattern visualization, and consistency evaluation.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Chain-of-Thought: A Latent Computational Mode in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of Chain-of-Thought prompting in triggering reasoning in large language models? Is CoT the unique mechanism or just one of several triggers for a latent reasoning capability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning in LLMs can be triggered by steering latent internal features identified via Sparse Autoencoders, indicating that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not the unique pathway but one of several triggers for an underlying reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in large language models can be triggered by activating latent internal features, showing that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not unique and that activation-level interventions are useful for understanding and controlling reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Steering a single reasoning-related latent feature improves reasoning accuracy without explicit Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Early single-feature steering leads to more concise reasoning outputs in large models, matching or exceeding CoT performance with fewer tokens.
The identified reasoning feature is activated early in generation and is associated with entering a reasoning mode rather than predicting answer correctness.
The reasoning feature generalizes across different prompts that encourage reasoning (e.g., 'Explain how', 'Solve carefully'), not just step-by-step prompts.
Random feature steering does not produce similar improvements, confirming the specificity of the identified reasoning-related feature.
papers.limitation: The identified SAE features are not fully disentangled or isolated reasoning mechanisms; conclusions are based on behavioral and intervention-level evidence, not complete mechanistic characterization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has improved the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), but it remains unclear why it works and whether it is the unique mechanism for triggering reasoning in large language models. In this work, we study this question by directly analyzing and intervening on the internal representations of LLMs with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), identifying a small set of latent features that are causally associated with LLM reasoning behavior. Across multiple model families and reasoning benchmarks, we find that steering a single reasoning-related latent feature can substantially improve accuracy without explicit CoT prompting. For large models, latent steering achieves performance comparable to standard CoT prompting while producing more efficient outputs. We further observe that this reasoning-oriented internal state is triggered early in generation and can override prompt-level instructions that discourage explicit reasoning. Overall, our results suggest that multi-step reasoning in LLMs is supported by latent internal activations that can be externally activated, while CoT prompting is one effective, but not unique, way of activating this mechanism rather than its necessary cause.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Unveiling Confirmation Bias in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does confirmation bias affect chain-of-thought reasoning behavior in LLMs, and why does its influence vary across questions, reasoning types, and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that confirmation bias is pervasive in LLMs' chain-of-thought reasoning, affecting both reasoning generation and answer prediction, and explains variance in CoT effectiveness across tasks and models.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that confirmation bias significantly impacts CoT reasoning in LLMs, explaining performance variance across tasks and models, and highlights the difficulty of debiasing strong beliefs.
papers.key_findings:
Internal beliefs (approximated by direct QA probabilities) significantly influence CoT performance at both reasoning generation and answer prediction stages.
Questions with stronger beliefs (lower entropy) are more likely to retain correctness regardless of difficulty, showing confirmation bias.
CoT improvement aligns with the degree to which tasks are prone to confirmation bias, with greater improvement on symbolic reasoning (e.g., math) than on non-symbolic tasks.
Models with weaker beliefs (higher entropy) are more sensitive to the quality and structure of the generated rationale.
Debiasing internal beliefs is challenging, especially when beliefs are strong, as models struggle to follow rationales that contradict their confident prior beliefs.
papers.limitation: The use of entropy as a proxy for belief strength limits analysis to white-box LLMs and multiple-choice questions.
future_direction: Explore confirmation bias using confidence measures applicable to black-box LLMs and open-ended questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been widely adopted to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).However, the effectiveness of CoT reasoning is inconsistent across tasks with different reasoning types.This work presents a novel perspective to understand CoT behavior through the lens of confirmation bias in cognitive psychology.Specifically, we examine how model internal beliefs, approximated by direct questionanswering probabilities, affect both reasoning generation (Q R) and reasoning-guided answer prediction (QR A) in CoT.By decomposing CoT into a two-stage process, we conduct a thorough correlation analysis in model beliefs, rationale attributes, and stage-wise performance.Our results provide strong evidence of confirmation bias in LLMs, such that model beliefs not only skew the reasoning process but also influence how rationales are utilized for answer prediction.Furthermore, the interplay between task vulnerability to confirmation bias and the strength of beliefs also provides explanations for CoT effectiveness across reasoning tasks and models.Overall, this study provides a valuable insight for the needs of better prompting strategies that mitigate confirmation bias to enhance reasoning performance.Code is available at https://github.com/yuewan2/biasedcot.

papers.title: Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: Does Huginn exhibit signs of latent chain-of-thought reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: We find limited evidence of interpretable latent chain-of-thought reasoning in the depth-recurrent transformer Huginn-3.5B, and uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks.
papers.conclusion: We find little evidence of structured latent chain-of-thought reasoning in Huginn, but it may be more subtle or distributed than our tools can detect.
papers.key_findings:
Probing inconsistencies across blocks in Huginn's depth-recurrent architecture: hidden state interpretability depends heavily on block index and decoding method.
Token rank trajectory analysis provides little evidence for latent CoT reasoning.
Scaling recurrence depth fails to match explicit reasoning: increasing recurrent steps only marginally improves performance and falls short of explicit CoT prompting.
papers.limitation: The results do not definitively rule out the presence of latent CoT; it may be more subtle or distributed than our employed tools can detect.
future_direction: Apply more advanced probing techniques, such as activation patching, to uncover finer-grained reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has enabled transformer-based language models to excel at complex mathematics and multi-step planning. However, in standard decoder-only architectures, these reasoning steps are externalized in natural language, improving interpretability at the cost of efficiency. To capture reasoning that is not easily represented in words, many works have explored recurrent architectures that aim to internalize reasoning in latent space, potentially supporting latent CoT. In this paper, we investigate whether such reasoning structures emerge in Huginn-3.5B, a depth-recurrent Transformer that reuses layers at inference time without increasing parameter count. We examine the model's internal behavior on arithmetic tasks using a suite of probing techniques including the Logit Lens and Coda Lens. Our findings reveal limited evidence of interpretable latent CoT by tracking rank trajectories of final and intermediate result tokens. Furthermore, we uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks, where the interpretability of hidden states depends heavily on both the layer index and the decoding method. Finally, we empirically show that increasing recurrence depth yields only marginal gains and falls well short of models that explicitly externalize reasoning steps. The code is available at https://github.com/wenquanlu/huginn-latent-cot.

papers.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
papers.research_question: Whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting faithfully reflects the true internal reasoning process of large language models.
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting induces more interpretable, causally effective, and sparser internal features in high-capacity LLMs, enhancing reasoning faithfulness, but this effect is scale-dependent and minimal in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompts induce more semantically coherent, causally effective, and sparser internal features in larger LLMs, but these effects are minimal in small models, highlighting the role of model capacity in reasoning faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoT improves feature interpretability and semantic coherence in larger models (Pythia-2.8B) but not in smaller ones (Pythia-70M).
Activation patching shows that CoT features have significant causal efficacy in larger models, improving answer log-probabilities when patched into noCoT runs.
CoT leads to sparser residual activations and SAE feature activations, especially in larger models.
Random feature patching often outperforms top-K patching in large models, indicating that useful CoT information is distributed across many features.
The benefits of CoT are scale-sensitive, with clear effects only in models above a certain size threshold.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching targets only the residual activation of the final token and does not trace causal effects through the reasoning process.
Interpretation module relies on OpenAI's LLM-based scoring, which offers an indirect perspective and is not grounded in specific neurons or heads.
Experiments are restricted to Pythia-2.8B and smaller variants; findings may not generalize to larger models.
SAE-based feature analysis may introduce biases and miss distributed or entangled representations.
future_direction: Conduct token-level and path-based causal analysis, such as stepwise interventions and path patching.
Develop activation-grounded and causally-validated explanation methods, including probing, clustering, and patching.
Scale the framework to larger models and diverse architectures, and explore subspace patching and automated circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting boosts Large Language Models accuracy on multi-step tasks, yet whether the generated "thoughts" reflect the true internal reasoning process is unresolved. We present the first feature-level causal study of CoT faithfulness. Combining sparse autoencoders with activation patching, we extract monosemantic features from Pythia-70M and Pythia-2.8B while they tackle GSM8K math problems under CoT and plain (noCoT) prompting. Swapping a small set of CoT-reasoning features into a noCoT run raises answer log-probabilities significantly in the 2.8B model, but has no reliable effect in 70M, revealing a clear scale threshold. CoT also leads to significantly higher activation sparsity and feature interpretability scores in the larger model, signalling more modular internal computation. For example, the model's confidence in generating correct answers improves from 1.2 to 4.3. We introduce patch-curves and random-feature patching baselines, showing that useful CoT information is not only present in the top-K patches but widely distributed. Overall, our results indicate that CoT can induce more interpretable internal structures in high-capacity LLMs, validating its role as a structured prompting method.

papers.title: Can Aha Moments Be Fake? Identifying True and Decorative Thinking Steps in Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do LLMs truly think through each verbalized step in their chain-of-thought (CoT)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the True Thinking Score (TTS) to quantify the causal contribution of each step in chain-of-thought reasoning, revealing that LLMs often interleave true-thinking steps with decorative ones, and identifies a steerable 'TrueThinking' direction in latent space that controls whether a step is internally followed.
papers.conclusion: LLMs often verbalize reasoning steps without performing them internally, challenging the efficiency of LLM reasoning and the trustworthiness of chain-of-thought as a safety-monitoring signal.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs often interleave true-thinking steps (which causally affect the final prediction) and decorative-thinking steps (which have minimal causal influence).
Only a small subset of reasoning steps causally drive the model's prediction; e.g., on AIME, only an average of 2.3% of steps have TTS ≥ 0.7 for Qwen-2.5.
Self-verification steps (aha moments) in CoT can be decorative, meaning the model does not truly check its solution internally.
A linear 'TrueThinking' direction in latent space can mediate whether LLMs internally reason over a verbalized step; steering along this direction forces engagement, while reversing it suppresses step use.
The latent signal controlling step engagement is universal across datasets and model sizes, with intermediate layers (e.g., 15-22 in Qwen) concentrating reasoning-related representations.
future_direction: Future study to explain the mechanisms of CoT reasoning and develop training objectives that reward reliance on true-thinking steps.
In-depth study of the geometry of hidden states and TrueThinking directions in the latent space.
papers.abstract: Large language models can generate long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but it remains unclear whether the verbalized steps reflect the models' internal thinking. In this work, we propose a True Thinking Score (TTS) to quantify the causal contribution of each step in CoT to the model's final prediction. Our experiments show that LLMs often interleave between true-thinking steps (which are genuinely used to compute the final output) and decorative-thinking steps (which give the appearance of reasoning but have minimal causal influence). We reveal that only a small subset of the total reasoning steps causally drive the model's prediction: e.g., on AIME, only an average of 2.3% of reasoning steps in CoT have a TTS >= 0.7 (range: 0-1) for Qwen-2.5. Furthermore, we find that LLMs can be steered to internally follow or disregard specific steps in their verbalized CoT using the identified TrueThinking direction. We highlight that self-verification steps in CoT (i.e., aha moments) can be decorative, while steering along the TrueThinking direction can force internal reasoning over these steps. Overall, our work reveals that LLMs often verbalize reasoning steps without performing them internally, challenging the efficiency of LLM reasoning and the trustworthiness of CoT.

papers.title: Deep Hidden Cognition Facilitates Reliable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Can the model’s internal activations effectively distinguish between truthful and false branches in CoT reasoning, and can these signals be used to guide more reliable CoT decoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method that leverages the model's internal truthfulness sensitivity, identified via probing attention heads, to train a confidence predictor. This predictor is then used to guide beam search during CoT generation, significantly enhancing the reliability of CoT reasoning by reducing error accumulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method, which leverages internal truthfulness signals to train a confidence predictor and guide CoT generation, significantly enhances the reliability of CoT reasoning across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
The model's internal activations during CoT reasoning encode truthfulness information, which can be extracted via probing attention heads.
A confidence predictor trained on these activations outperforms baselines like sequence likelihood and verbalized confidence in calibration metrics.
Integrating the confidence predictor into a beam search framework for CoT generation improves reasoning accuracy across diverse unimodal and multimodal tasks and model scales.
The method is compatible with self-correction techniques and generalizes to specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1.
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning has demonstrated remarkable deep reasoning capabilities in both large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, its reliability is often undermined by the accumulation of errors in intermediate steps. This paper introduces an novel approach to calibrate the CoT reasoning accuracy by leveraging the model's intrinsic veracity encoding. We discover that specific attention head activations reliably reflect the truthfulness of reasoning steps in CoT. Based on this insight, we train a confidence predictor to evaluate the correctness of each reasoning step using these truthfulness-sensitive activations, dynamically selecting the most plausible reasoning path via beam search. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Few-Shot CoT, Self-Consistency, and Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search) across the mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning tasks, exhibiting superior accuracy and reliability in both unimodal and multimodal settings. We further validate the approach on large reasoning models, confirming its applicability to specialized reasoning models. Additionally, we explore the role of the model's self-correction ability in CoT reasoning. This work provides a novel reliability improvement path for CoT reasoning with broad application potential.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning emerge in transformers, and what are the inner workings and conditions for its appearance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers through the identification and analysis of a specialized attention mechanism called an 'iteration head', which enables efficient iterative reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve iterative tasks efficiently via CoT reasoning by developing inner circuits (iteration heads) dedicated to multistep reasoning, and data curation can guide this process.
papers.key_findings:
Iteration heads, a specific pattern of weights in the first two attention layers, emerge in transformers trained on iterative tasks with CoT.
These heads enable the transformer to solve iterative tasks efficiently by retrieving the current input and previous state to compute the next state.
The iterative reasoning skill granted by iteration heads is transferable between different iterative tasks (e.g., from copying to parity).
Data curation (including easier tasks in training) can guide the model towards learning the iteration head circuit.
Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a limitation for complex iterative algorithms.
papers.limitation: Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a shortcoming for complex iterative algorithms or generic language modeling.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power. However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited. This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting. In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads". We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models: Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting in large language models? Specifically, does the model merely mimic exemplars, what changes occur in the projection space (logits), and does CoT enable deeper and broader utilization of pre-trained knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This work analyzes the internal mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting, finding that LLMs imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with question understanding, exhibit fluctuating but ultimately more concentrated logits distributions, and activate a broader set of neurons in final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought prompting enhances LLM reasoning by guiding models to imitate exemplar formats, focus logits distributions, and activate a broader set of knowledge-related neurons, leading to more accurate and confident answers.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs imitate the format of CoT exemplars (e.g., using sequence words like 'first', 'then') while generating personalized responses based on their understanding of the question.
During CoT generation, token logits fluctuate more than with standard prompts, but the final answer generation shows a more concentrated logits distribution, suggesting clearer direction.
CoT prompts lead to a broader range and higher intensity of neuron activations in the final layers compared to standard prompts, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval from pre-training.
Successful imitation of transferred CoT prompts correlates with higher answer accuracy, suggesting that understanding the exemplar format is key to CoT's effectiveness.
The probability distribution over candidate answers at the answer generation step is more concentrated (lower entropy) under CoT prompting, indicating higher model confidence in the selected answer.
papers.limitation: Experiments were conducted on a limited sample of 50 test examples per dataset due to budget constraints.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more models and tasks.
Explore the dynamic changes in neuron activations across different layers.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models, with numerous studies exploring factors influencing its performance. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. To further demystify the operational principles, this work examines three key aspects: decoding, projection, and activation, aiming to elucidate the changes that occur within models when employing Chainof-Thought. Our findings reveal that LLMs effectively imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with their understanding of the question, exhibiting fluctuations in token logits during generation but ultimately producing a more concentrated logits distribution, and activating a broader set of neurons in the final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval compared to standard prompts. Our code and data will be publicly avialable when the paper is accepted.

papers.title: A Hopfieldian View-based Interpretation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: For zero-shot CoT, why does prompting the model with 'let's think step by step' significantly impact its outputs? For few-shot CoT, why does providing examples before questioning the model substantially improve its reasoning ability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework based on the Hopfieldian view to interpret Chain-of-Thought reasoning, enabling error localization and control to correct reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides intuitive and interpretable analysis for CoT reasoning, which is helpful in tracing and controlling errors made during the CoT process, rectifying reasoning paths, and enhancing transparency.
papers.key_findings:
The framework can decipher the inner workings of CoT reasoning.
It provides reasoning error localization by reading concept-specific representations.
It controls the reasoning direction to rectify errors and improve accuracy.
The approach answers why zero-shot and few-shot CoT prompts improve reasoning.
Experimental results on seven datasets across three tasks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness.
papers.limitation: The current problem formulation is primarily focused on text data.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-modal scenarios.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) holds a significant place in augmenting the reasoning performance for large language models (LLMs). While some studies focus on improving CoT accuracy through methods like retrieval enhancement, yet a rigorous explanation for why CoT achieves such success remains unclear. In this paper, we analyze CoT methods under two different settings by asking the following questions: (1) For zero-shot CoT, why does prompting the model with "let's think step by step" significantly impact its outputs? (2) For few-shot CoT, why does providing examples before questioning the model could substantially improve its reasoning ability? To answer these questions, we conduct a top-down explainable analysis from the Hopfieldian view and propose a Read-and-Control approach for controlling the accuracy of CoT. Through extensive experiments on seven datasets for three different tasks, we demonstrate that our framework can decipher the inner workings of CoT, provide reasoning error localization, and control to come up with the correct reasoning path.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Computations in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do transformer models internally process and represent reasoning steps when Chain-of-Thought is replaced with filler characters, and can these hidden characters be recovered?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that hidden characters in filler Chain-of-Thought sequences can be recovered by analyzing layer-wise representations and token rankings without loss of performance, providing insights into internal mechanisms of transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on how models internally process and represent reasoning steps when explicit chain of thought is obscured, contributing to model interpretability and opening avenues for improving transparency in language model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise analysis reveals that filler tokens emerge in later layers, overwriting earlier numerical representations.
Token ranking analysis shows that original reasoning tokens remain among lower-ranked candidates beneath filler tokens.
A modified decoding algorithm can recover hidden characters by selecting non-filler tokens when fillers are top-ranked, without compromising task performance.
The model performs necessary computations in earlier layers and then overwrites intermediate representations with filler tokens in later layers to match training targets.
The findings suggest that models retain hidden reasoning steps internally even when outputting filler tokens.
papers.limitation: Focuses on a synthetic task (3SUM) and a relatively small transformer model, which may not capture complexities of real-world language tasks and larger models.
future_direction: Explore whether specific circuits, such as induction heads or particular attention patterns, are involved in overwriting behavior.
Apply similar analysis techniques to other tasks and models to assess the generality of the findings.
Extend the investigation to natural language tasks and larger models to determine if observed phenomena persist in more complex settings.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, recent studies have shown that models can still perform complex reasoning tasks even when the CoT is replaced with filler(hidden) characters (e.g., "..."), leaving open questions about how models internally process and represent reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate methods to decode these hidden characters in transformer models trained with filler CoT sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representations using the logit lens method and examining token rankings, we demonstrate that the hidden characters can be recovered without loss of performance. Our findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of transformer models and open avenues for improving interpretability and transparency in language model reasoning.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: Reasoning aligns language models to human cognition
papers.research_question: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an active probabilistic reasoning task that disentangles sampling from inference, and a mechanistic model with four latent cognitive variables, showing that chain-of-thought reasoning improves inference quality and shifts LLMs toward human-like decision strategies.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning shifts language models toward human-like evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
Extended reasoning (chain-of-thought) is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference quality while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling.
Reasoning shifts LLMs toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference.
LLMs with extended reasoning can match or exceed humans in inference quality but still underperform in sampling quality compared to skilled humans.
A mechanistic model with four interpretable latent variables (Memory, Strategy, Choice Bias, Occlusion Awareness) captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior and places humans and models in a shared cognitive space.
The model fits reveal that chain-of-thought reasoning reduces inference loss and partially aligns sampling strategies, but a gap in information acquisition remains.
papers.abstract: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do, and what role does chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We introduce an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence toward a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary large language models against near-optimal reference policies reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference and producing belief trajectories that become strikingly human-like, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a mechanistic model that captures systematic deviations from optimal behavior via four interpretable latent variables: memory, strategy, choice bias, and occlusion awareness. This model places humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space, reproduces behavioral signatures across agents, and shows how chain-of-thought shifts language models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, tightening alignment in inference while leaving a persistent gap in information acquisition.

papers.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) help transformers recover a world model in the form of finite state automata (FSAs), or do they merely learn shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer+CoT learns implicit finite state automata (FSAs) for state tracking, as evidenced by mechanistic analysis showing that late-layer MLP neurons implement state transitions and exhibit compression and distinction properties.
papers.conclusion: Transformer+CoT achieves near-perfect next-token prediction while internalizing an FSA-like structured state representation, bridging the gap between theoretical expressiveness and practical learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer+CoT efficiently learns state tracking for sequences of arbitrary length across multiple groups (Z60, A4 × Z5, A5), outperforming other architectures like RNNs and transformer variants.
The circuit for state tracking relies heavily on late-layer MLP neurons, with MLP11 playing a key role.
Neurons in late-layer MLPs can be classified into states based on transition rules with high accuracy, indicating an N-to-1 mapping between neurons and states.
The model exhibits near-perfect compression and distinction metrics, providing evidence that it recovers an implicit FSA structure.
The learned FSAs are robust to skipping intermediate steps and noise in scratchpads, but struggle with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
papers.limitation: The model struggles with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
future_direction: Modifications to model architecture, loss functions, or optimization algorithms to improve length generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks, and prior research shows that CoT can theoretically increase expressiveness. However, there is limited mechanistic understanding of the algorithms that Transformer+CoT can learn. Our key contributions are: (1) We evaluate the state tracking capabilities of Transformer+CoT and its variants, confirming the effectiveness of CoT. (2) Next, we identify the circuit (a subset of model components, responsible for tracking the world state), indicating that late-layer MLP neurons play a key role. We propose two metrics, compression and distinction, and show that the neuron sets for each state achieve nearly 100% accuracy, providing evidence of an implicit finite state automaton (FSA) embedded within the model. (3) Additionally, we explore three challenging settings: skipping intermediate steps, introducing data noises, and testing length generalization. Our results demonstrate that Transformer+CoT learns robust algorithms (FSAs), highlighting its resilience in challenging scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/IvanChangPKU/FSA.

papers.title: Knowing Before Saying: LLM Representations Encode Information About Chain-of-Thought Success Before Completion
papers.research_question: Can the success of a zero-shot Chain-of-Thought process be predicted before completion, and do LLMs encode information about reasoning success in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal representations encode information about Chain-of-Thought success before generation, and a probing classifier can predict success, enabling potential early stopping.
papers.conclusion: The success of CoT reasoning can be predicted from LLM internal representations before generation, and these findings may inform methods to make CoT more efficient without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
A probing classifier based on LLM internal representations can predict CoT success before any token generation with 60% to 76.4% accuracy.
Internal representations outperform a BERT baseline that relies on generated tokens, indicating they encode deeper reasoning dynamics.
Providing later reasoning steps does not always improve prediction accuracy, and when it doesn't, earlier representations are more similar to later ones.
Early stopping experiments show that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.
The model's intermediate representations may encode sufficient information for correct answers, but zero-shot early stopping is suboptimal.
papers.limitation:
The test set for Mistral-7B was annotated by GPT-4o mini, which may be less reliable than human annotation, and results should be interpreted with caution.
Zero-shot early stopping is a suboptimal intervention because the model does not always converge to a stable answer even when nearly the entire reasoning sequence is generated.
future_direction: Using supervised learning to train the model to generate concise reasoning chains.
Using reinforcement learning to reinforce brevity via rewards.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether the success of a zeroshot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be predicted before completion.We discover that a probing classifier, based on LLM representations, performs well even before a single token is generated, suggesting that crucial information about the reasoning process is already present in the initial steps representations.In contrast, a strong BERT-based baseline, which relies solely on the generated tokens, performs worse-likely because it depends on shallow linguistic cues rather than deeper reasoning dynamics.Surprisingly, using later reasoning steps does not always improve classification.When additional context is unhelpful, earlier representations resemble later ones more, suggesting LLMs encode key information early.This implies reasoning can often stop early without loss.To test this, we conduct early stopping experiments, showing that truncating CoT reasoning still improves performance over not using CoT at all, though a gap remains compared to full reasoning.However, approaches like supervised learning or reinforcement learning designed to shorten CoT chains could leverage our classifier's guidance to identify when early stopping is effective.Our findings provide insights that may support such methods, helping to optimize CoT's efficiency while preserving its benefits.

papers.title: How Chain-of-Thought Works? Tracing Information Flow from Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting alter a model's internal states to improve reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: CoT works by constraining the decoding space via answer templates, with structural adherence strongly correlating with performance, and modulates neuron activation in a task-dependent manner (reducing activation in open-domain tasks, increasing it in closed-domain tasks).
papers.conclusion: The findings provide a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for designing more efficient and robust CoT prompts.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompts models to imitate structural keywords (e.g., 'time', 'action') from the prompt and content keywords (e.g., numbers) from the input question.
There is a strong positive correlation between adherence to the CoT reasoning structure (measured by Imitation Count) and task performance (accuracy).
CoT leads to more concentrated probability distributions (lower entropy) and higher confidence in generated tokens compared to standard prompting.
CoT reduces the average number of activated neurons in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for open-domain tasks, but increases it for closed-domain tasks, indicating task-dependent modulation of neural engagement.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting significantly enhances model reasoning, yet its internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. We analyze CoT's operational principles by reversely tracing information flow across decoding, projection, and activation phases. Our quantitative analysis suggests that CoT may serve as a decoding space pruner, leveraging answer templates to guide output generation, with higher template adherence strongly correlating with improved performance. Furthermore, we surprisingly find that CoT modulates neuron engagement in a task-dependent manner: reducing neuron activation in open-domain tasks, yet increasing it in closed-domain scenarios. These findings offer a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for enabling targeted CoT interventions to design more efficient and robust prompts. We released our code and data at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cot-D247.

papers.title: Do Latent-CoT Models Think Step-by-Step? A Mechanistic Study on Sequential Reasoning Tasks
papers.research_question: Does latent chain-of-thought (specifically CODI) implement genuine step-by-step reasoning on sequential tasks, or does it rely on shortcuts and late-stage fusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that latent CoT (CODI) implements step-by-step reasoning only for short hops (2-3) and shifts to a partial, late-bottleneck strategy for longer tasks, with performance and mechanism depending on the compressibility of the task (composite vs prime moduli).
papers.conclusion: With composite moduli, CODI is step-by-step on 2–3 hops but shifts to a late-intermediate partial rollout on longer horizons; with prime moduli, it largely fails to learn and shows neither signature. The split is explained by compressibility: composite moduli induce many-to-one contractions that bias the label toward late updates, making the computation compressible, while prime moduli lack this structure.
papers.key_findings:
For 2-3 hop polynomial tasks, CODI forms bridge states in the latent channel and fuses them with the final input at the answer readout.
For longer hop tasks (n>=4), CODI collapses to a partial latent rollout, representing only the last one or two intermediate states.
There is a prime-composite split: under composite moduli, CODI succeeds with a late-bottleneck strategy; under prime moduli, performance drops and step-by-step reasoning fails.
The final input is routed directly to the answer readout via a copy-like pathway, separate from the latent channel.
Teacher-guided compression drives the partial-reasoning strategy under composite moduli.
